headline: Rates Hold Near Two-Week Low as Yields Tick Up
tileReason: The latest daily 30-year average is 7.26%, a two-week low from Wednesday, but the 10-year Treasury yield is up about 0.05% this morning as stocks rebound and oil climbs in a shortened holiday session.
takeaway:
Mortgage rates start Friday near a two-week low. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average was last at 7.26% on Wednesday, down from 7.32% Tuesday; bond markets were closed Thursday for Thanksgiving, so there has been no new daily reading since. Freddie Mac's weekly survey sits at 7.21%, and the Mortgage Research Center shows about 7.10%.

Treasury yields are edging up this morning as stocks bounce back. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, was near 4.90% at 9:15 AM ET, up about 0.05% from Wednesday's close of about 4.85% to 4.86%, ending an eight-day slide for now. Stock futures jumped about 2% overnight as chip and AI shares rebounded, and when investors move back into stocks they sell some of the bonds they bought for safety, which pushes yields up.

Oil is adding a little upward pressure. Crude prices rose about 1% this morning after reported Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities, and higher energy costs can feed inflation, which tends to push rates up. A government report showed October's goods trade deficit widened to about $149.5 billion, larger than expected, but it is the only data out today and rarely moves rates much.

Today is a short, thin holiday session. Bond markets close early at 2 PM ET for the day after Thanksgiving, and with many traders out, moves can be choppy and don't always stick. Lenders who change their rate sheets today would be reacting to this morning's modest rise in yields.

A December Fed hike looks all but certain. Futures markets (where traders bet on the Fed's next move) put the odds of a quarter-point increase on Dec 9 at about 99% this morning, with about 1% on no change; one outlet cited 95%, so readings vary a little. Odds of another hike in January are around 59%. These are market expectations, not a Fed forecast.

Lenders still have a cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 17, the latest day recorded, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room is part of why lenders have been able to pass along recent bond rallies.

The big tests come next week and the week after. Next up are the Dec 1 factory survey and job openings, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

drivers.title: Stocks rebound, pulling money out of bonds
drivers.text: Stock futures jumped about 2% overnight as chip and AI shares bounced back. When investors return to stocks they sell some of the safe-haven Treasuries they bought, which lifts yields; the 10-year was near 4.90% this morning, up about 0.05%.

drivers.title: Oil climbs after attacks on Saudi energy sites
drivers.text: Crude rose about 1% this morning after reported Houthi strikes on Saudi energy facilities. Higher oil prices can feed inflation, which tends to push yields and mortgage rates up.

drivers.title: December Fed hike all but locked in
drivers.text: Futures odds of a quarter-point Fed hike on Dec 9 are about 99%, and markets see roughly a 59% chance of another in January. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term rates have a hard time falling far.

drivers.title: Recent bond rally still lowers the starting point
drivers.text: The 10-year fell eight straight trading days through Wednesday, to about 4.85%, as tech stocks slid, which brought the daily 30-year mortgage average down to 7.26%, a two-week low. This morning's uptick only gives back a small part of that.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 17, the latest day recorded, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap gives lenders room to pass along bond rallies.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 25 close (latest reading; markets closed Nov 26 and today's reading not yet out)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even, tilted slightly higher. Rates are at a two-week low after an eight-day Treasury rally, and the gap between mortgage rates and Treasuries is still wide (about 2.19% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), which leaves room for lenders to cut. Working against borrowers: yields are bouncing this morning as stocks rebound, oil is climbing, core inflation came in a bit hot, the economy still looks strong and a December Fed hike is all but priced in. Big swing events: the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and its projections, Dec 10 consumer prices, the stock market and oil headlines.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

calendar.label: Fri, Nov 20
calendar.event: Final November consumer sentiment (University of Michigan); Fed Governors Waller (8:25 AM ET) and Cook (12:15 PM ET) speak
calendar.why: Consumers' inflation expectations feed into the Fed's thinking, and Fed comments about more hikes can push rates up.
calendar.actual: 51.5; consumers expect 3.7% inflation over the next year, down from 4.3% early this month, and 3.3% over five years
calendar.surpriseLabel: in line, with lower inflation expectations
calendar.reaction: Stocks fell 3.7% and the 10-year yield dropped about 0.12% to near 4.92%, and lenders cut mortgage rates during the day.

calendar.label: Mon, Nov 23
calendar.event: November business surveys (S&P Global flash PMIs); $69B 2-year note sale; New York Fed President Williams speaks
calendar.why: Williams is one of the Fed's most influential voices, so any hint about the pace of hikes can move rates.
calendar.actual: Williams said inflation near 3.5% is too high and he wouldn't rule out back-to-back hikes; 2-year notes sold at about 4.70%; Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and the S&P 500 jumped 4.7%
calendar.reaction: The 10-year yield jumped early on the stock rally, then settled about unchanged near 4.92% as oil fell; mortgage rates edged up 0.01%.

calendar.label: Tue, Nov 24
calendar.event: Consumer confidence (Conference Board) and September home prices; $70B 5-year note sale (10 AM PT)
calendar.why: Strong confidence points to a sturdy economy and spending, which tends to push rates up.
calendar.actual: 103.3, highest since January 2025; Case-Shiller 20-city home prices +2.6% from a year earlier (2.7% expected); 5-year notes sold at 4.719%
calendar.reaction: Bonds held up as tech stocks fell; the 10-year ended near 4.91% and the 30-year mortgage average slipped 0.02% to 7.32%.

calendar.label: Wed, Nov 25
calendar.event: October PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred measure), income and spending, Q3 growth revision, durable goods orders and jobless claims (8:30 AM ET); MBA weekly survey; new home sales (10 AM ET); $44B 7-year note sale; Freddie Mac weekly survey (noon ET); Fed Beige Book (2 PM ET)
calendar.why: Hotter inflation would add to the case for more Fed hikes and push rates up.
calendar.actual: PCE 0.3% monthly (3.8% yearly); core 0.3% (3.3% yearly); Q3 growth revised to 4.3% from 3.4%; jobless claims 189K, down 13K; durable goods orders +0.2%; new home sales 701K pace, up 14.2%; MBA 30-year 7.38%, purchase applications +10%; Freddie Mac 30-year 7.21%; Beige Book: 8 of 12 districts growing slightly to moderately, prices still rising moderately
calendar.reaction: Yields fell anyway, a move that began before the reports as tech stocks slid; the 10-year ended near 4.86%, mortgage bond prices rose about 0.29 and the 30-year mortgage average fell 0.06% to 7.26%.

calendar.label: Fri, Nov 27
calendar.event: October advance trade and inventory figures (8:30 AM ET); bond market closes early at 2 PM ET (SIFMA)
calendar.why: A quiet holiday session; thin trading can make moves choppy.
calendar.actual: Goods trade deficit $149.5B, wider than September's $135.1B (revised); wholesale inventories +0.9%, retail inventories +0.8%
calendar.reaction: Little reaction; the 10-year yield was near 4.90% by 9:15 AM ET, up about 0.05%, mostly on the stock rebound.

calendar.why: Signs the economy or job market is cooling tend to pull rates down.

calendar.label: Thu, Dec 10

talkingPoints.buyers: Mortgage rates are near a two-week low, with the daily 30-year average last at 7.26% and Freddie Mac's weekly survey at 7.21%. Treasury yields are ticking up this morning as stocks rebound, and a December Fed hike looks nearly certain, so the picture can shift quickly. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates are at their lowest in two weeks, around 7.26%, and purchase mortgage applications rose about 10% in the latest week. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out over the holidays.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates are holding near a two-week low around 7.26% after Thanksgiving, though Treasury yields are edging up this morning as stocks bounce back.
